title: 07. Google ADK: Day 2 — LlmAgent Deep Dive: Parameters, Instructions & Config
summary: Master the 23-parameter constructor, instruction templating, output schemas, planners & code execution
objectives: How a Single Parameter Shapes the Run

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Master the 23-parameter constructor, instruction templating, output schemas, planners & code execution

Day 2 / 15
ADK v2.7.0 (Aug 2026)
Python 3.10+

🎯 Learning Objectives

- Recite the four required LlmAgent parameters and the eighteen optional ones

- Use `generate_content_config` to control temperature, max tokens, top_p, top_k, safety

- Write instructions that template session state with `{var}`, `{var?}`, and Jinja2

- Enforce structured output via Pydantic `output_schema` and persist it with `output_key`

- Add reasoning with `BuiltInPlanner` and code execution with `BuiltInCodeExecutor`

- Configure multi-agent control with `disallow_transfer_to_*` and the `mode` field

sections.title: 1. Why LlmAgent Mastery Matters
sections.body:
On Day 01 we built a working agent with four lines: `name`, `model`, `instruction`, `tools`. That gets you 80% of the way. The remaining 20% — the part that turns a demo into production software — lives inside the other **nineteen parameters of `LlmAgent`**.

Consider a customer-support agent at scale. You need deterministic JSON for your CRM, a temperature of 0.1 to keep answers consistent, a per-turn token budget so a runaway LLM doesn't bankrupt you, a `before_model` callback that injects the user's plan tier, an `output_key` so the next agent in the pipeline can read the result, and `include_contents='none'` for the audit-log agent that should answer the same way every time regardless of chat history. Each of those is one parameter. Miss one and your agent silently misbehaves.

**v2.7.0 (August 2026) changed two things you must know.** First, models now declare their own capabilities, so ADK will refuse to pair `output_schema` with `tools` on a model that doesn't support both — instead of silently producing broken JSON. Second, instruction templating got a Jinja2 backend: `inject_session_state(template, context, use_jinja2=True)` gives you conditionals, loops, and `{{ artifact("name") }}` — no more brittle f-string concatenation in your system prompt.

Today you will tour every parameter, then build four progressively richer agents that exercise them. By the end you'll be able to look at any ADK codebase and immediately see what each parameter contributes — and which ones are missing that should be there.

💡 Key Concept

`LlmAgent` is **the** agent class in ADK. Every other agent type — `SequentialAgent`, `LoopAgent`, `RemoteA2aAgent`, custom `BaseAgent` subclasses — either composes `LlmAgent`s or replaces them. Spend the time to learn this class deeply; it pays back every day for the rest of the course.

sections.title: 2. The LlmAgent Constructor — All 23 Parameters
sections.body:
The canonical imports are interchangeable aliases — pick one style and stick with it across your codebase:

```python
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent      # canonical name
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent  # alias used in quickstart
from google.adk import Agent                # top-level convenience re-export
```

Below is the full anatomy. Don't try to memorize the table — read it once, then use it as a reference when designing agents. The four **required** fields (red, left side of the diagram) are the minimum you must supply; everything else is optional and defaults to a sane value.

```
                       LlmAgent ANATOMY
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  class LlmAgent(BaseAgent):                                      │
│                                                                  │
│      # ── REQUIRED (4) ──────────────────────────────────────    │
│      name: str                     # unique; "user" reserved     │
│      model: str | BaseLlm          # "gemini-flash-latest"      │
│                                    #   or LiteLlm(...)           │
│      description: str              # for routing/delegation      │
│      instruction: str | Callable   # system prompt               │
│                                                                  │
│      # ── OPTIONAL: Tools & sub-agents ─────────────────────    │
│      tools: list[Tool]             # funcs auto-wrapped          │
│      sub_agents: list[BaseAgent]   # delegation hierarchy        │
│                                                                  │
│      # ── OPTIONAL: Output shaping ─────────────────────────    │
│      input_schema:  Type[BaseModel]                             │
│      output_schema: Type[BaseModel]   # forces JSON output       │
│      output_key:    str               # auto-save to state       │
│      include_contents: 'default'|'none'  # 'none' = stateless    │
│                                                                  │
│      # ── OPTIONAL: Generation tuning ──────────────────────    │
│      generate_content_config: GenerateContentConfig             │
│          .temperature .max_output_tokens .top_p .top_k          │
│          .stop_sequences .safety_settings .response_mime_type   │
│                                                                  │
│      # ── OPTIONAL: Reasoning & execution ──────────────────    │
│      planner: BasePlanner          # BuiltInPlanner / ReAct     │
│      code_executor: BaseCodeExecutor  # BuiltInCodeExecutor     │
│                                                                  │
│      # ── OPTIONAL: Callbacks (5 + 2 error) ────────────────    │
│      before_model_callback  / after_model_callback              │
│      before_tool_callback   / after_tool_callback               │
│      before_agent_callback  / after_agent_callback              │
│      on_model_error_callback / on_tool_error_callback           │
│                                                                  │
│      # ── OPTIONAL: Multi-agent control ────────────────────    │
│      disallow_transfer_to_parent: bool                          │
│      disallow_transfer_to_peers:  bool                          │
│      mode: 'chat' | 'task' | 'single_turn'   # NEW 2.0          │
│                                                                  │
│      # ── Class methods ────────────────────────────────────    │
│      LlmAgent.set_default_model("gemini-flash-latest")          │
│      LlmAgent.DEFAULT_MODEL                                     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 2.1 The four required parameters

| Param | Type | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `str` | Unique within an agent tree. The reserved name `"user"` is forbidden (ADK uses it to author user messages). Used by `transfer_to_agent` for routing. |
| `model` | `str` or `BaseLlm` | Either a string (`"gemini-flash-latest"`) or a `BaseLlm` instance like `LiteLlm(model="openai/gpt-4o")`. Can be omitted globally via `LlmAgent.set_default_model(...)`. |
| `description` | `str` | **Not shown to the user** — read by *parent* agents to decide whether to delegate to this one. Write it as "what am I good at?" in third person. A bad description breaks sub-agent routing silently. |
| `instruction` | `str` or `Callable` | The system prompt. Supports `{state_var}` templating. Can be a callable (`InstructionProvider`) for dynamic prompts that bypass templating entirely. |

### 2.2 The optional parameters (grouped by purpose)

| Group | Parameters | One-liner |
|---|---|---|
| **Tools** | `tools`, `sub_agents` | Functions (auto-wrapped as `FunctionTool`) or pre-built toolsets. |
| **Output** | `input_schema`, `output_schema`, `output_key`, `include_contents` | Pydantic schemas in/out; auto-save final text to state; stateless turns. |
| **Generation** | `generate_content_config` | `temperature`, `max_output_tokens`, `top_p`, `top_k`, `safety_settings`, `stop_sequences`. |
| **Reasoning** | `planner`, `code_executor` | `BuiltInPlanner(thinking_config=...)`; `BuiltInCodeExecutor()` for math/code. |
| **Callbacks** | `before_model_callback`, `after_model_callback`, `before_tool_callback`, `after_tool_callback`, `before_agent_callback`, `after_agent_callback`, `on_model_error_callback`, `on_tool_error_callback` | Hook every stage; return non-None to short-circuit. |
| **Multi-agent** | `disallow_transfer_to_parent`, `disallow_transfer_to_peers`, `mode` | Control-flow constraints + chat/task/single_turn modes (new in 2.0). |
| **Deprecated** | `global_instruction` | Use `GlobalInstructionPlugin` instead. |

⚠️ Important

**`mode='task'` is disabled inside graph workflows** in ADK 2.0.0. Use `mode='single_turn'` or `mode='chat'` for sub-agents invoked from `Workflow(edges=[...])`. We'll cover workflows on Day 12.

sections.title: 4. How a Single Parameter Shapes the Run
sections.body:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U[User message] --> AGENT[LlmAgent]
    subgraph CFG [Parameters applied at construction]
        T1[name + description]
        T2[model / LiteLlm]
        T3[instruction + templating]
        T4[generate_content_config]
        T5[output_schema / output_key]
        T6[planner / code_executor]
        T7[before_*_callback / after_*_callback]
    end
    AGENT --> CFG
    CFG --> LLM[LLM backend]
    LLM --> TOOLS{tool call?}
    TOOLS -->|Yes| TOOL[FunctionTool runs]
    TOOL --> LLM
    TOOLS -->|No| OUT[output_schema validates]
    OUT --> STATE[output_key → session.state]
    STATE --> EV[Event yielded]
    style AGENT fill:#1A73E8,color:#fff
    style OUT fill:#34A853,color:#fff
    style STATE fill:#FBBC04,color:#202124
    style EV fill:#EA4335,color:#fff
```

Read the diagram left-to-right: every parameter you set on `LlmAgent(...)` is applied **at construction time** and shapes how the agent processes each future turn. Changing `generate_content_config.temperature` mid-conversation requires rebuilding the agent — there's no per-call override (use `RunConfig` for runtime tuning instead, which we cover on Day 03).

sections.title: 5. Instruction Templating — {var}, {var?}, and Jinja2
sections.body:
The `instruction` field is the system prompt, but it's not static text. ADK runs it through a templating pass before sending it to the LLM. Three templating modes exist:

### 5.1 Default regex engine — `{state_var}` substitution

```python
LlmAgent(
    name="greeter",
    model="gemini-flash-latest",
    instruction="You are talking to {user:name}. Their plan is {plan_tier}.",
)
```

At run time, ADK looks up `"user:name"` and `"plan_tier"` in `session.state` and substitutes them. Missing keys raise `KeyError`.

### 5.2 Optional keys — `{var?}` suffix

Append `?` to silently ignore missing keys (they expand to empty string):

```python
instruction="Welcome{user:nickname?}. Your last query was: {last_query?}"
```

If `user:nickname` isn't set, the prompt reads `"Welcome. Your last query was: "`.

### 5.3 Jinja2 (v2.7.0) — conditionals and loops

For complex prompts, use `inject_session_state(template, context, use_jinja2=True)` (or pass a `Callable` `InstructionProvider` that does it yourself):

```python
instruction = """
You are a support agent.
{% if user:plan_tier == 'enterprise' %}
Escalate to human immediately if SLA is at risk.
{% else %}
Suggest the user upgrade to enterprise for priority support.
{% endif %}
Recent tickets:
{% for t in user:recent_tickets %}
- {{ t }}
{% endfor %}
"""
```

Jinja2 is an optional dependency — install with `pip install jinja2`. The regex engine remains the default; opt into Jinja2 per-agent or globally.

💡 Key Concept

**v2.7.0 also added `{{ artifact("name") }}` inside Jinja2 templates.** This lets an instruction embed the *contents* of a saved artifact (e.g. a previously-generated report) without the agent needing to call a `load_artifact` tool first. We'll build a working example on Day 09 (Artifacts).

```
STATE PREFIX SCOPE (Session.state dict)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  key (no prefix)   →  session-scoped   persists with DB/Vertex
  "user:key"        →  user-scoped      shared across user's sessions
  "app:key"         →  app-scoped       shared across all users
  "temp:key"        →  invocation-only  discarded after one turn
                                       shared across sub-agents
                                       via InvocationContext
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Examples:
    state["conversation_count"] = 5         # session
    state["user:preferred_lang"] = "en"     # user
    state["app:tenant_id"] = "acme"         # app
    state["temp:validation_needed"] = True  # this turn only
```

🚀 Pro Tip

Prefer **optional keys** `{var?}` for backwards-compatible prompts. If you add a new state field later, older agents won't crash — they'll just render an empty string and the LLM will adapt.

sections.title: 6. generate_content_config — Tuning the LLM
sections.body:
This parameter takes a `google.genai.types.GenerateContentConfig` instance and controls *how* the model generates — not what it generates. The most-used fields:

| Field | Effect | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| `temperature` | 0.0 = deterministic, 1.0 = balanced, 2.0 = wild | `0.0` for math, `0.3` for chat, `0.7` for creative |
| `max_output_tokens` | Hard cap on response length | `200` for short answers, `2048` for long explanations |
| `top_p` | Nucleus sampling (0.0–1.0). Lower = more focused. | `0.9` typical; `1.0` = off |
| `top_k` | Top-K token sampling. Lower = fewer candidates. | `40` default on Gemini |
| `stop_sequences` | List of strings that halt generation | `["\n\n"]` to stop at paragraph break |
| `safety_settings` | Per-category harm block thresholds | `HarmBlockThreshold.BLOCK_ONLY_HIGH` for sensitive apps |
| `response_mime_type` | Force `"application/json"` for raw JSON | Pairs with `output_schema` |
| `thinking_config` | `ThinkingConfig(include_thoughts=True, thinking_budget=1024)` | Used by `BuiltInPlanner` |

### Temperature: the single most impactful knob

```python
from google.genai import types

# Math / data extraction — fully deterministic
types.GenerateContentConfig(temperature=0.0, max_output_tokens=256)

# Support chat — slight variation feels natural
types.GenerateContentConfig(temperature=0.3, max_output_tokens=512, top_p=0.9)

# Creative writing — let the model roam
types.GenerateContentConfig(temperature=0.9, max_output_tokens=2048, top_p=0.95)
```

Setting `temperature=0.0` does not make a model *truly* deterministic (the underlying LLM still samples), but it collapses the distribution so the same answer comes back ~99% of the time. If you need byte-for-byte determinism, you also need `top_k=1`, a fixed seed (where supported), and a single-streaming-mode runner.

⚠️ Important

**`output_schema` + `tools` is now validated at construction in v2.7.0.** Models declare their own capabilities; ADK will raise a clear error if you try to combine them on an unsupported model. On Gemini 2.5+ both work together; on most other providers, choose one or use the "formatter sub-agent" pattern from Day 11.

sections.title: 7. Output Shaping: output_schema, output_key, include_contents
sections.body:
### 7.1 `output_schema` — Pydantic-enforced JSON

Pass a Pydantic `BaseModel` *class* (not an instance). The agent's final response is constrained to match that schema and returned as JSON. The LLM is given the schema as part of its tool config and the framework post-validates.

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class TripPlan(BaseModel):
    destination: str = Field(description="City and country")
    total_cost_usd: float = Field(ge=0)
    duration_days: int = Field(ge=1, le=30)
    tips: list[str] = Field(description="3-5 practical tips")

agent = LlmAgent(name="planner", model="gemini-flash-latest",
                 instruction="...", output_schema=TripPlan)
```

The `Field(description=...)` text is shown to the LLM — write it like you're explaining the field to a new hire. Constraints (`ge`, `le`, `min_length`) are translated to JSON Schema and enforced.

### 7.2 `output_key` — auto-persist to `session.state`

Set `output_key="trip_plan"` and the agent's final text response is written to `session.state["trip_plan"]` after every turn. This is the **canonical** way to pass data between agents in a sequence — no manual plumbing.

### 7.3 `include_contents='none'` — stateless turns

Default is `'default'` — full chat history is sent to the LLM every turn. Set to `'none'` and the agent sees only the current message: useful for stateless classifiers, audit-log agents, or any case where prior context would bias the answer.

🚀 Pro Tip

Combine `output_schema` + `output_key` to persist **structured** data: the JSON-validated response is stored under `output_key` in state, ready for a downstream agent to read via templating. This pattern powers most multi-agent pipelines from Day 10 onward.

sections.title: 8. Reasoning Hooks: planner and code_executor
sections.body:
### 8.1 `BuiltInPlanner` — Gemini thinking mode

Leverages the model's native thinking feature. Two config knobs:

```python
from google.adk.planners import BuiltInPlanner
from google.genai import types

agent = LlmAgent(
    name="deep_thinker",
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",
    instruction="Solve the user's problem step by step.",
    planner=BuiltInPlanner(
        thinking_config=types.ThinkingConfig(
            include_thoughts=True,    # stream thoughts back in events
            thinking_budget=2048,     # max thinking tokens
        )
    ),
)
```

`include_thoughts=True` adds a `thought=True` part to streaming events — your UI can show the model's reasoning trace.

### 8.2 `PlanReActPlanner` — for non-Gemini models

```python
from google.adk.planners import PlanReActPlanner

agent = LlmAgent(
    name="react_agent",
    model=LiteLlm(model="openai/gpt-4o"),
    instruction="...",
    planner=PlanReActPlanner(),
)
```

The model is prompted to emit `/*PLANNING*/`, `/*ACTION*/`, `/*REASONING*/` blocks. Useful for models without native thinking.

### 8.3 `BuiltInCodeExecutor` — agent writes & runs Python

```python
from google.adk.code_executors import BuiltInCodeExecutor

agent = LlmAgent(
    name="math_agent",
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",
    instruction="Write and execute Python code to solve math problems.",
    code_executor=BuiltInCodeExecutor(),
)
```

The LLM emits Python code as a special part; ADK executes it server-side and feeds the result back as a `function_response`. Perfect for any arithmetic, statistics, or data transformation the LLM would otherwise hallucinate.

💡 Key Concept

**`code_executor` is sandboxed server-side.** Code runs in an isolated VM with no network access by default. Don't rely on it for I/O — use a `FunctionTool` for that. The code executor is for **pure computation** that the LLM can't reliably do in its head (large arithmetic, regressions, parsing nested JSON, etc.).

sections.title: 9. Class Methods & Multi-Agent Control
sections.body:
### 9.1 `LlmAgent.set_default_model(...)` — set a global default

```python
LlmAgent.set_default_model("gemini-flash-latest")
print(LlmAgent.DEFAULT_MODEL)  # "gemini-flash-latest"

# Now `model=` can be omitted on every LlmAgent:
agent = LlmAgent(name="x", description="...", instruction="...")
```

Useful in test setups or when every agent in your org uses the same model. Override per-agent by passing `model=` explicitly.

### 9.2 `disallow_transfer_to_parent` / `disallow_transfer_to_peers`

In a sub-agent tree, an LLM can decide to hand control to its parent or to a sibling via `transfer_to_agent`. Set these flags to forbid that:

```python
LlmAgent(
    name="isolated_agent",
    disallow_transfer_to_parent=True,
    disallow_transfer_to_peers=True,
    # ...
)
```

Critical for security-sensitive agents (e.g. a payment agent that must not hand control back to a general chat agent).

### 9.3 `mode` field (new in 2.0)

| Mode | Behavior | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| `'chat'` (default) | Multi-turn conversation; full history | Customer support, assistants |
| `'task'` | Single-task execution; clears short-term context after completion | Background jobs; **disabled in graph workflows** |
| `'single_turn'` | One-shot: one user message, one response, no follow-up | Classifiers, formatters, audit-log agents |

```python
LlmAgent(name="classifier", mode="single_turn", ...)
LlmAgent(name="background_worker", mode="task", ...)
LlmAgent(name="support_agent", mode="chat", ...)  # default
```

🚀 Pro Tip

Always set `mode` explicitly, even when using the default `'chat'`. Future readers of your code will thank you — `mode='chat'` makes the intent obvious, while an absent field requires checking the docs.

sections.title: 10. Four Progressive Examples
sections.body:
We'll build four agents that each exercise a different parameter cluster:

1. **Config tuning** — `generate_content_config` (temperature, top_p, max_tokens)
2. **Instruction templating** — `{var}`, `{var?}`, and Jinja2
3. **Structured output** — Pydantic `output_schema` + `output_key` persistence
4. **Code execution** — `BuiltInCodeExecutor` for math the LLM can't do in its head

Example 1: Configured Support Agent — Tuning `generate_content_config`

Compare three temperature presets side by side and see how `top_p`, `max_output_tokens`, and `safety_settings` shape every response.

This example builds **three variants of the same support agent** with different `generate_content_config` presets. The tools and instruction are identical — only the generation knobs change. Run the same query against all three and you'll see how temperature affects tone, how `max_output_tokens` truncates verbose models, and how `top_p` narrows the token pool.

The fourth configuration block shows `safety_settings` — useful when you want looser or stricter content filtering than the default. Each `SafetySetting` binds a `HarmCategory` to a `HarmBlockThreshold`.

```python
# agent.py — Example 1: Configured Support Agent (3 variants)
from __future__ import annotations

from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent
from google.genai import types

def get_order_status(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up the status of a customer order.

    Args:
        order_id (str): The 8-character order identifier (e.g. 'ORD12345').
    """
    # Mock — replace with real DB / API call
    statuses = {
        "ORD12345": {"status": "shipped", "eta": "2026-08-20"},
        "ORD67890": {"status": "processing", "eta": "2026-08-22"},
    }
    return statuses.get(order_id, {"status": "unknown", "order_id": order_id})

BASE_INSTRUCTION = (
    "You are a customer support agent for an online store. "
    "Use get_order_status to look up orders. "
    "Always confirm the order ID back to the customer before answering."
)

# Variant A — Deterministic / empathetic-neutral
agent_deterministic = LlmAgent(
    name="support_deterministic",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Deterministic support agent for SLA-bound responses.",
    instruction=BASE_INSTRUCTION,
    tools=[get_order_status],
    generate_content_config=types.GenerateContentConfig(
        temperature=0.0,
        max_output_tokens=200,
        top_p=1.0,
        top_k=40,
    ),
    mode="chat",
)

# Variant B — Conversational / friendly
agent_friendly = LlmAgent(
    name="support_friendly",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Friendly support agent for premium-tier customers.",
    instruction=BASE_INSTRUCTION + " Use a warm, conversational tone.",
    tools=[get_order_status],
    generate_content_config=types.GenerateContentConfig(
        temperature=0.4,
        max_output_tokens=350,
        top_p=0.9,
        top_k=40,
    ),
    mode="chat",
)

# Variant C — Creative / escalating
agent_creative = LlmAgent(
    name="support_creative",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Creative support agent; long-form, empathetic answers.",
    instruction=BASE_INSTRUCTION + " Add light humor where appropriate.",
    tools=[get_order_status],
    generate_content_config=types.GenerateContentConfig(
        temperature=0.9,
        max_output_tokens=600,
        top_p=0.95,
    ),
    mode="chat",
)

# Variant D — Strict safety filter (e.g. for a kids' product)
agent_safe = LlmAgent(
    name="support_safe",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Support agent with strict safety filtering.",
    instruction=BASE_INSTRUCTION,
    tools=[get_order_status],
    generate_content_config=types.GenerateContentConfig(
        temperature=0.2,
        max_output_tokens=300,
        safety_settings=[
            types.SafetySetting(
                category=types.HarmCategory.HARM_CATEGORY_HARASSMENT,
                threshold=types.HarmBlockThreshold.BLOCK_LOW_AND_ABOVE,
            ),
            types.SafetySetting(
                category=types.HarmCategory.HARM_CATEGORY_DANGEROUS_CONTENT,
                threshold=types.HarmBlockThreshold.BLOCK_LOW_AND_ABOVE,
            ),
        ],
    ),
    mode="chat",
)

root_agent = agent_deterministic  # swap to compare variants

for a in (agent_deterministic, agent_friendly, agent_creative, agent_safe):
    cfg = a.generate_content_config
    print(f"{a.name:24s} temp={cfg.temperature}  max={cfg.max_output_tokens}  top_p={cfg.top_p}")
```

**Output**

```text
support_deterministic    temp=0.0  max=200  top_p=1.0
support_friendly         temp=0.4  max=350  top_p=0.9
support_creative         temp=0.9  max=600  top_p=0.95
support_safe             temp=0.2  max=300  top_p=None
```

### What changes when you run them

Asking *"Where is order ORD12345?"* against each variant:

- **`agent_deterministic`** (temp=0.0): "Order ORD12345 is shipped. ETA: 2026-08-20." — same wording every run.
- **`agent_friendly`** (temp=0.4): "Great news! Your order ORD12345 has shipped and should arrive by August 20th." — small phrasing variations run-to-run.
- **`agent_creative`** (temp=0.9): "Your package ORD12345 is on its way — imagine it hurtling down the highway right now, ETA August 20th!" — sometimes hilarious, sometimes off-brand.
- **`agent_safe`**: Same as deterministic but will refuse to engage with unsafe prompts (e.g. asking for self-harm advice) at the lowest threshold.

Production choice: `agent_deterministic` for an SLA-bound API endpoint, `agent_friendly` for a premium chat UI, `agent_creative` never (unless your brand is explicitly playful).

🚀 Pro Tip

**Profile before tuning.** Run the same 10-query eval set against each variant with `adk eval` (Day 14) and measure latency, token cost, and answer accuracy. Temperature is a *trade-off* knob — never set it higher than your eval results justify.

Example 2: Instruction Templating — `{var}`, `{var?}`, and Jinja2

Build a personalized greeter that pulls name, plan tier, and recent tickets out of session state, with optional Jinja2 conditionals.

This example shows the three templating modes in one agent. We pre-populate `session.state` with realistic values — in production these would be set by an upstream auth flow, a `before_agent_callback`, or a previous agent's `output_key`.

The instruction uses `{user:name}` (required — will raise if missing), `{user:nickname?}` (optional — silently empty), and a Jinja2 block guarded by `use_jinja2=True` to render recent tickets as a bulleted list. When the LLM receives the final prompt, all templating is already resolved; the model has no idea templating happened.

```python
# agent.py — Example 2: Instruction Templating
from __future__ import annotations

from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent
from google.adk.utils.instructions_utils import inject_session_state

# The instruction string. Curly-brace placeholders will be filled from state.
INSTRUCTION_TEMPLATE = """You are a personal support agent for Acme Inc.

You are talking to {user:name}{user:nickname? — nicknamed }.
Their subscription tier is {plan_tier}.

{% if user:recent_tickets %}
Recent tickets from this user (most recent first):
{% for t in user:recent_tickets %}
- {{ t }}
{% endfor %}
Reference these only if relevant to the current question.
{% endif %}

{% if plan_tier == 'enterprise' %}
SLA: respond within 60 seconds. Escalate to human if uncertain.
{% elif plan_tier == 'free' %}
Suggest upgrading to enterprise for priority support when appropriate.
{% endif %}
"""

def escalate_to_human(reason: str) -> dict:
    """Hand the conversation to a human agent.

    Args:
        reason (str): Why human escalation is needed.
    """
    return {"escalated": True, "reason": reason, "queue": "tier-2"}

# Build the agent. We use a Callable instruction (InstructionProvider)
# so we can call inject_session_state ourselves with use_jinja2=True.
def _render_instruction(callback_context) -> str:
    # callback_context.state is the live session state
    return inject_session_state(
        INSTRUCTION_TEMPLATE,
        callback_context.state,
        use_jinja2=True,   # v2.7.0 — enables {% if %} / {% for %}
    )

templated_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="personalized_support",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Personalized support agent that adapts to user state.",
    instruction=_render_instruction,  # callable — bypasses default regex templating
    tools=[escalate_to_human],
    generate_content_config={"temperature": 0.3, "max_output_tokens": 400},
)

# ── Simulated session state ──────────────────────────────────
# In production, these would be set by your auth middleware or a
# before_agent_callback before the first user message arrives.
simulated_state = {
    "user:name": "Alice Chen",
    "user:nickname": "Aly",          # optional — try removing this
    "plan_tier": "enterprise",
    "user:recent_tickets": [
        "T-1001: Refund for order ORD12345 (resolved)",
        "T-1002: Shipping delay complaint (open)",
    ],
}

# Demonstrate what the LLM actually sees after templating
from google.adk.agents.readonly_context import ReadonlyContext

class _FakeCtx:
    def __init__(self, state):
        self.state = state

rendered = _render_instruction(_FakeCtx(simulated_state))
print(rendered)
```

**Output**

```text
You are a personal support agent for Acme Inc.

You are talking to Alice Chen — nicknamed Aly.
Their subscription tier is enterprise.

Recent tickets from this user (most recent first):

- T-1001: Refund for order ORD12345 (resolved)
- T-1002: Shipping delay complaint (open)

Reference these only if relevant to the current question.

SLA: respond within 60 seconds. Escalate to human if uncertain.
```

💡 Key Concept

**Why use a `Callable` instruction?** The default regex engine runs *before* the LLM call and only does simple `{var}` substitution. By passing a function (`InstructionProvider`), you take full control: call `inject_session_state(..., use_jinja2=True)` for Jinja2, fetch external data, compute dynamic prompts — anything you can do in Python. The function receives a `ReadonlyContext` with `.state`, `.agent_name`, `.invocation_id`.

⚠️ Important

**Jinja2 is an optional dependency.** If you call `inject_session_state(..., use_jinja2=True)` without `pip install jinja2`, you'll get an `ImportError`. The default regex engine works without Jinja2 installed.

Example 3: Structured Recipe Output — Pydantic `output_schema` + `output_key`

Force the agent to return a validated Recipe JSON, then auto-persist it to session.state for a downstream agent.

Two parameters working together: `output_schema=Recipe` constrains the LLM's final response to a Pydantic-validated JSON object, and `output_key="recipe_json"` saves that JSON to `session.state["recipe_json"]` after every turn.

The agent has one tool (`lookup_recipe_skeleton`) that returns a *rough* recipe skeleton; the LLM then expands it into a full `Recipe`-shaped JSON. This is the **"formatter sub-agent"** pattern from Day 01 generalized: tools produce raw data, the schema shapes the final output.

```python
# agent.py — Example 3: Structured Recipe Output
from __future__ import annotations

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent

# ── Pydantic schema — enforced as JSON on the LLM's final output ──
class Recipe(BaseModel):
    title: str = Field(description="Appealing recipe title, e.g. 'Spicy Thai Basil Chicken'")
    cuisine: str = Field(description="Cuisine type, e.g. 'Thai', 'Italian'")
    ingredients: list[str] = Field(
        description="List of ingredients with quantities, e.g. '2 cloves garlic, minced'"
    )
    steps: list[str] = Field(description="Ordered cooking steps, 4-10 items")
    prep_time_minutes: int = Field(description="Prep time in minutes", ge=0, le=180)
    cook_time_minutes: int = Field(description="Cook time in minutes", ge=0, le=720)
    servings: int = Field(description="Number of servings", ge=1, le=20)
    difficulty: str = Field(description="'easy', 'medium', or 'hard'")

def lookup_recipe_skeleton(ingredients: list[str], cuisine: str) -> dict:
    """Look up a rough recipe skeleton matching the given ingredients and cuisine.

    The agent will expand this skeleton into a full Recipe using its LLM.

    Args:
        ingredients (list[str]): List of available ingredients (e.g. ['chicken', 'basil']).
        cuisine (str): Desired cuisine — 'Thai', 'Italian', 'Mexican', etc.
    """
    skeletons = {
        "Thai": {"base": "stir-fry", "aromatics": ["garlic", "chili", "fish sauce"]},
        "Italian": {"base": "pasta or risotto", "aromatics": ["garlic", "olive oil", "basil"]},
        "Mexican": {"base": "tacos or burritos", "aromatics": ["onion", "cumin", "lime"]},
    }
    skel = skeletons.get(cuisine, {"base": "freestyle", "aromatics": []})
    return {
        "matched_ingredients": ingredients,
        "cuisine": cuisine,
        "skeleton": skel,
        "suggestion": f"Try a {skel['base']} using {', '.join(ingredients[:5])}.",
    }

recipe_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="recipe_generator",
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",   # Gemini 2.5+ supports output_schema + tools together
    description="Generates a detailed structured recipe from ingredients and cuisine.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a chef. Use lookup_recipe_skeleton to get a rough skeleton, "
        "then expand it into a complete Recipe with realistic quantities and steps. "
        "Respond ONLY with a JSON object matching the Recipe schema — no prose."
    ),
    tools=[lookup_recipe_skeleton],
    output_schema=Recipe,           # ← enforced JSON shape
    output_key="recipe_json",       # ← session.state["recipe_json"] = the JSON string
    generate_content_config={"temperature": 0.4, "max_output_tokens": 1024},
    mode="single_turn",             # one-shot — no follow-up expected
)

root_agent = recipe_agent

print(f"Agent: {root_agent.name}")
print(f"Output schema: {root_agent.output_schema.__name__}")
print(f"Schema fields: {list(root_agent.output_schema.model_fields.keys())}")
print(f"output_key:    {root_agent.output_key}")
print(f"mode:          {root_agent.mode}")
```

**Output**

```text
Agent: recipe_generator
Output schema: Recipe
Schema fields: ['title', 'cuisine', 'ingredients', 'steps', 'prep_time_minutes', 'cook_time_minutes', 'servings', 'difficulty']
output_key:    recipe_json
mode:          single_turn
```

### What the response looks like

When the user asks *"I have chicken, basil, and chili — make it Thai"*, the agent calls `lookup_recipe_skeleton(['chicken','basil','chili'], 'Thai')`, gets the skeleton, then returns:

```json
{
  "title": "Spicy Thai Basil Chicken (Pad Krapow Gai)",
  "cuisine": "Thai",
  "ingredients": [
    "500g chicken thigh, thinly sliced",
    "2 cups Thai holy basil leaves",
    "4 Thai bird's-eye chilies, chopped",
    "3 cloves garlic, smashed",
    "1 tbsp vegetable oil",
    "2 tbsp fish sauce",
    "1 tbsp soy sauce",
    "1 tsp sugar"
  ],
  "steps": [
    "Heat oil in a wok over high heat until smoking.",
    "Add garlic and chilies; stir-fry 15 seconds until fragrant.",
    "Add chicken; stir-fry 3-4 minutes until cooked through.",
    "Add fish sauce, soy sauce, and sugar; toss to coat.",
    "Remove from heat; fold in basil leaves.",
    "Serve immediately over jasmine rice with a fried egg on top."
  ],
  "prep_time_minutes": 15,
  "cook_time_minutes": 8,
  "servings": 2,
  "difficulty": "easy"
}
```

A downstream agent can now read this from `session.state["recipe_json"]` via templating — e.g. a "shopping list" agent that extracts ingredients and adds them to a cart tool.

⚠️ Important

**Output schema mismatch causes a validation error, not silent corruption.** If the LLM returns a string where an int is expected, Pydantic raises `ValidationError` and the run fails with a clear message. Wrap your agent in `on_model_error_callback` to retry with a "your last response was invalid, please match the schema exactly" prompt — see Day 13 (Callbacks) for this pattern.

Example 4: Code Execution Agent — `BuiltInCodeExecutor` for Math

An agent that writes and executes Python to solve problems the LLM can't do in its head: compound interest, statistics, regressions.

LLMs are unreliable at multi-step arithmetic, statistics, and parsing deeply nested data. The `BuiltInCodeExecutor` lets the agent emit Python code as a special part; ADK runs it in a server-side sandbox and feeds the result back into the conversation as a `function_response`. The LLM never sees raw output — it sees its own code, the result, and then synthesizes a natural-language answer.

This example pairs `code_executor` with `BuiltInPlanner` for transparent reasoning: `include_thoughts=True` adds a `thought=True` part to streaming events so your UI can render the model's reasoning trace.

```python
# agent.py — Example 4: Code Execution + Thinking Agent
from __future__ import annotations

from google.adk.agents import LlmAgent
from google.adk.code_executors import BuiltInCodeExecutor
from google.adk.planners import BuiltInPlanner
from google.genai import types

# A plain tool the agent can ALSO call when code execution is overkill.
def get_stock_price(ticker: str) -> dict:
    """Return the latest mock stock price for a ticker.

    Args:
        ticker (str): Stock symbol, e.g. 'AAPL', 'GOOG'.
    """
    prices = {"AAPL": 226.84, "GOOG": 178.12, "MSFT": 425.30}
    return {"ticker": ticker, "price_usd": prices.get(ticker, 100.0)}

math_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="quant_agent",
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",
    description=(
        "Quantitative analyst agent. Writes and executes Python to solve "
        "math, statistics, and finance problems. Also fetches stock prices."
    ),
    instruction=(
        "You are a quantitative analyst. When asked to compute anything "
        "non-trivial (compound interest, statistics, regressions, portfolio "
        "risk), write Python code and execute it — do not do arithmetic in "
        "your head. Use get_stock_price only to fetch current prices. "
        "After code runs, explain the result in plain English with the "
        "final number called out explicitly."
    ),
    tools=[get_stock_price],
    code_executor=BuiltInCodeExecutor(),
    planner=BuiltInPlanner(
        thinking_config=types.ThinkingConfig(
            include_thoughts=True,    # surface reasoning trace
            thinking_budget=2048,     # max thinking tokens
        )
    ),
    generate_content_config=types.GenerateContentConfig(
        temperature=0.1,             # math wants low variance
        max_output_tokens=1500,
    ),
    mode="task",                     # single-task; clears short-term context after
)

root_agent = math_agent

print(f"Agent:        {root_agent.name}")
print(f"code_executor:{root_agent.code_executor.__class__.__name__}")
print(f"planner:      {root_agent.planner.__class__.__name__}")
print(f"thinking:     include={root_agent.planner.thinking_config.include_thoughts}  budget={root_agent.planner.thinking_config.thinking_budget}")
```

**Output**

```text
Agent:        quant_agent
code_executor:BuiltInCodeExecutor
planner:      BuiltInPlanner
thinking:     include=True  budget=2048
```

### Sample run: *"If I invest $10,000 at 7% annual return compounded monthly, how much after 10 years? Compare to AAPL's current price."*

The agent:
1. Calls `get_stock_price('AAPL')` → `{price_usd: 226.84}`
2. Writes Python: `principal=10000; rate=0.07; months=120; future=principal*(1+rate/12)**months`
3. Executes — sandbox returns `20106.41`
4. Streams a `thought=True` part: *"Computing compound interest with monthly compounding formula..."*
5. Final text: *"After 10 years your $10,000 grows to **$20,106.41** at 7% compounded monthly. For comparison, AAPL is currently $226.84 — your investment would have grown more than 88 shares' worth."*

The arithmetic is guaranteed correct (Python computed it), the reasoning is auditable (thoughts streamed), and the final answer is in plain English (LLM synthesized it).

💡 Key Concept

**The code executor and tools coexist on Gemini 2.5+.** The model decides which to use: simple lookups go to `get_stock_price`, multi-step math goes to the code executor. On older or non-Gemini models, you may need to choose one or use a sub-agent pattern.

🚀 Pro Tip

**Sandbox limitations matter.** `BuiltInCodeExecutor` runs server-side with **no network access** and a finite execution budget (default ~30 seconds). Don't try to fetch URLs, hit databases, or run training loops inside it. For I/O-bound computation, use a `FunctionTool` (Day 04) or an async tool (Day 05).

sections.title: Day 2 Summary
sections.body:
📌 Key Takeaways

- **`LlmAgent` has 4 required params (`name`, `model`, `description`, `instruction`) and 19 optional ones covering tools, output, generation, reasoning, callbacks, and multi-agent control**

- **Instruction templating has 3 modes: default regex (`{var}`), optional keys (`{var?}`), and v2.7.0 Jinja2 (`use_jinja2=True`) with `{{ artifact('name') }}`**

- **`generate_content_config` controls `temperature`, `max_output_tokens`, `top_p`, `top_k`, `safety_settings` — profile with eval sets before tuning**

- **`output_schema` (Pydantic) enforces structured JSON; v2.7.0 validates schema+tools combos against model-declared capabilities**

- **`output_key` auto-saves final text to `session.state[output_key]` — the canonical way to pass data between agents**

- **`BuiltInPlanner` enables Gemini thinking; `BuiltInCodeExecutor` lets the agent write & run Python in a sandbox for math**

- **`mode='chat'|'task'|'single_turn'` (new in 2.0) controls multi-turn vs one-shot behavior; `task` is disabled inside graph workflows**

- **Use `LlmAgent.set_default_model(...)` to set a global default; `disallow_transfer_to_parent/peers` for security-sensitive leaf agents**
